764.title: The laugh in Maya's hall
764.hook: Duryodhana is fooled by Maya's hall and laughed at, and a host's duty to a guest is broken
764.carry: atithi devo bhava: the guest is god
764.howItsDone: Many Hindu homes still greet a guest with water, a seat and food, following atithi devo bhava; and some storytellers treat Duryodhana's humiliation in Maya's hall as the opening of the dice-game story.

segments.voice: Yesterday a light rose from Shishupala and entered Krishna, and the Rajasuya was finished: what the mind dwells on, it reaches.

The guests have gone home, but one has stayed behind. Duryodhana lingers at Indraprastha with his uncle Shakuni, wandering through the great hall the asura builder Maya made for the Pandavas. It's a hall of wonders, and wonders can be tricky. Floors that look like water. Water that looks like floor. Doors that seem open and aren't. A new story starts here, the dice game. But it doesn't start with dice. It starts with a man walking through a beautiful room and getting it wrong, again and again.
screen: `ONE GUEST STAYS BEHIND.` → `MAYA'S HALL OF WONDERS.` → `IT STARTS WITHOUT DICE.`

segments.voice: In the telling, Duryodhana comes to a spot on the floor that looks like a pool. It's crystal, but he takes it for water and gathers up his clothes to wade across. Nothing wet. Then he comes to a real pool, so clear it looks like solid floor, and walks straight in, clothes and all. Bhima sees it, and laughs. The servants laugh too. Yudhishthira, the host, sends him dry clothes. By the end, the hall has fooled him over and over, and his mistakes have had an audience. Now, the teaching. Hindu homes keep an old line, from the Taittiriya Upanishad: atithi devo bhava, let the guest be a god to you. That's why so many families meet a visitor with water, a seat, and far too much food. In Maya's hall the line is tested. Yudhishthira keeps it: his guest is soaked, so he covers him. Bhima forgets it: his guest is soaked, so he laughs. Many teachers read the moment this way: the dice game, and the war after it, open from a guest shamed in the house that should have sheltered him. The poem doesn't excuse what Duryodhana does next. It shows where the wound opened. Today it's the same small test. Someone at your table spills, mispronounces a dish, walks into the wrong room. Yudhishthira's way is to hand them the dry clothes before anyone gets to laugh.

segments.voice: Picture someone coming to your door this week: a friend, a neighbor, someone you don't know well. In your mind, do what Hindu homes have done for centuries: open the door, offer a glass of water, offer a seat, and let them feel like the most important person in the room. Then remember one time a guest of yours was embarrassed, and see yourself handing them the dry clothes. If you pray, you can bring that guest into your prayer; if not, simply wish them ease.

765.title: Envy on the road home
765.hook: on the road home, Duryodhana confesses his envy to Shakuni, and Shakuni turns it into a plan
765.carry: envy is one of the six inner enemies
765.howItsDone: In Hindu retellings of the Mahabharata, Shakuni is known as the master of the dice, and the conversation on the road is told as the moment Duryodhana's envy becomes a plan.

segments.voice: Yesterday the dice game began without dice: a guest fooled by Maya's hall, and laughed at. Atithi devo bhava, the guest is god.

Duryodhana is heading home to Hastinapura, and he keeps sighing. His uncle Shakuni, riding with him, notices and asks what's wrong. And Duryodhana tells him. Not a polite version. The whole thing: the kings bowing to his cousin, the wealth flowing in, the hall that made a fool of him, the laughter. He says he can't bear it. He says it's burning him up inside. A confession on the road, and an uncle who hears in it an opportunity.
screen: `SIGHING ON THE ROAD HOME.` → `SHAKUNI ASKS.` → `THE WHOLE THING POURS OUT.`

segments.voice: Listen to what Duryodhana actually says. Not that the Pandavas cheated him. That they're prospering, and he can't stand it. Their success is the injury. Shakuni at first does what a good friend might: don't grieve, he says; they have their fortune, you have yours. But Duryodhana won't be comforted. So Shakuni changes course. You can't beat them in battle, he says in effect; they're too strong. But Yudhishthira loves dice, and doesn't play well. I do. Invite him to a game, and I'll win everything he has, and you won't lift a weapon. Now the teaching. Hindu teachers have a name for what's burning in Duryodhana. They speak of six inner enemies, the shadripu: kama, desire; krodha, anger; lobha, greed; moha, delusion; mada, pride; and matsarya, envy. They're called enemies, not sins, because they live inside you and fight you for the wheel. And the Mahabharata gives envy a face. Many readers see Duryodhana as the epic's great portrait of matsarya: a prince with a kingdom of his own, made miserable by someone else's good fortune, until the feeling finds a helper and becomes a plan. That's the teaching for today. You won't stop envy from arriving; a cousin's news, a friend's win, and there it is. The Hindu move is to name the enemy when it shows up, before it finds its Shakuni.

segments.voice: Is there someone whose good fortune is hard to watch right now, a friend's news, a sibling's easy road? Let the name come, and call the sting what Hindu teachers call it: matsarya, envy, an enemy inside, not the truth about them or you. Then say for them a prayer many Hindus know: sarve bhavantu sukhinah, may all be happy. Say it slowly, with their name in it. If you don't pray, simply wish them well, three times, and mean it a little more each time.
Envy, matsarya in Sanskrit, the last of the six inner enemies: taking someone else's good fortune as your own wound. Today Duryodhana speaks it aloud, and Shakuni answers with a plan.

766.title: Vidura's warning
766.hook: the blind king hears Vidura warn against the game, blames fate, and says yes anyway
766.carry: karma: calling it fate doesn't undo the choice
766.howItsDone: In Hindu retellings, Vidura is remembered as a voice of wise counsel at the Kuru court, the one who tells the blind king what he doesn't want to hear.

segments.voice: Yesterday, on the road home, Duryodhana spoke his envy aloud, and Shakuni offered a plan to win without a war. Envy is one of the six inner enemies.

A plan needs permission. Duryodhana is a prince, not the king. To invite Yudhishthira to anything, the invitation has to come from his father, Dhritarashtra, the blind king of Hastinapura. So uncle and nephew go to the palace. Shakuni speaks first, gently, about how pale and thin the prince has grown. And the king, who loves his son, asks him what's wrong. The plan moves from a road to a throne room, and a father has to decide.
screen: `A PLAN NEEDS PERMISSION.` → `TO THE BLIND KING.` → `A FATHER ASKS WHAT'S WRONG.`

segments.voice: Duryodhana tells his father what he told Shakuni, and Shakuni lays out the game. Dhritarashtra hesitates. In the telling, he wants to ask Vidura first, his wise half-brother. Duryodhana pushes back hard: ask Vidura, and Vidura will stop it. He presses until his father gives way. So the king orders a splendid hall built for the game, and only then calls Vidura, not to ask, but to tell him. Vidura says plainly that he doesn't approve: this game will set the cousins against each other. And Dhritarashtra answers, in effect: if the gods are kind, no harm will come; what is fated will happen. Then he sends Vidura himself to bring Yudhishthira to play. Now the teaching. Hindu teaching on karma is not that everything is fixed. Karma means action, and the fruit that follows it. Some of what reaches us is the ripening of the past, yes. But the choice in front of you is yours, and it makes new karma. Many teachers read Dhritarashtra's line about fate as the moment he hides a choice behind a word. He heard the warning. He loved his son too much to refuse him, and called it destiny. The epic doesn't let him off; the rest of the poem is the fruit of that yes. For today: when you hear yourself say whatever happens, happens, about something you could still change, that's Dhritarashtra talking. Karma says the choice is still on your desk.
screen: `DHRITARASHTRA HESITATES.` · `VIDURA WARNS: IT WILL END IN QUARREL.` · `WHAT IS FATED WILL HAPPEN.` · `KARMA: ACTION, AND ITS FRUIT.` · then, large: `CALLING IT FATE DOESN'T UNDO THE CHOICE.`

segments.voice: Think of a time you said yes to someone you love when part of you wanted to say no, and picture the moment you gave way. Notice if you told yourself it was out of your hands. Now say it the karma way, quietly: that was my choice, and I can choose again. No guilt; just ownership. If you pray, you can offer that choice, and that person, in your prayer; if not, simply hold them in mind.
Vidura. The counselor who warns that this game will end in quarrel, and is sent anyway, by a father who called his own choice fate.
Your line: karma, calling it fate doesn't undo the choice. Dhritarashtra heard Vidura, and said yes. See you tomorrow.

767.title: Before the first throw
767.hook: Yudhishthira calls the game deceit, Shakuni dares him, and a vow walks him to the board
767.carry: keeping a rule isn't the same as dharma
767.howItsDone: The dice scene is retold in homes, on stage and on screen, and the talk before the first throw is a place where readers and listeners stop to argue about Yudhishthira's choice.

segments.voice: Yesterday the blind king heard Vidura's warning, called it fate, and sent for Yudhishthira anyway. Calling it fate doesn't undo the choice.
screen: `CALLING IT FATE DOESN'T UNDO THE CHOICE.`

segments.voice: The new hall is ready, and Yudhishthira has come. The guests are seated, the cloth is spread, and the dice are out. Before anyone throws, there's a conversation, and it's easy to hurry past it on the way to the drama. Don't. Everything that follows is already folded inside it. Yudhishthira says plainly what he thinks of this kind of game. Shakuni answers him, and the answer has a hook in it. And a choice gets made in the open, before the elders have even taken their seats.
screen: `THE BOARD IS SET.` → `A CONVERSATION FIRST.` → `A CHOICE MADE IN THE OPEN.`

segments.voice: Shakuni opens: the hall is full; it's time to play. Yudhishthira doesn't pretend. Gambling of this kind is deceit, he says; there's no warrior's courage in it. Shakuni's answer is clever: a skilled player beats an unskilled one, and nobody calls that cheating. Then the sting: if you're afraid, don't play. Yudhishthira's reply is the hinge. Called to play, I don't turn back; that's my vow. And fate rules everyone. Duryodhana says his uncle will throw for him. Yudhishthira sees that it's unfair, says so, and agrees anyway. The elders take their seats with heavy hearts. The first stake, a pearl set in gold. Shakuni throws, and wins. Now the teaching. Yudhishthira isn't just any king. Hindus call him Dharmaraja, the king of dharma; the epic makes him a son of the god Dharma himself. And here the man of dharma is walked to the board by a rule. That's the hard Hindu lesson the epic keeps teaching: dharma is subtle. It isn't a list of rules kept no matter what. It's what upholds, what holds a family and a world together. A vow is a good thing; Hindus keep vratas, vows and fasts, all the time. But a vow serves dharma, not the other way round. Some readers call Yudhishthira's choice integrity; others call it pride. Either way, the rule he kept led to ruin. For today: when a rule you keep starts hurting what it was meant to protect, dharma asks you to look again.
screen: `YUDHISHTHIRA: THIS GAME IS DECEIT.` · `CALLED TO PLAY, I DON'T TURN BACK.` · `THE FIRST STAKE: A PEARL SET IN GOLD.` · `DHARMARAJA, WALKED TO THE BOARD BY A RULE.` · then, large: `A VOW SERVES DHARMA.`

segments.voice: Say quietly to yourself a rule you keep and are a little proud of: I always finish what I start, I never say no to family, I don't back down. Then ask it the dharma question: does this rule still hold up the people it's meant to protect? Don't drop it or defend it; hold it to the light for a few breaths. If you pray, bring it into your prayer; if not, let the breath carry it.
Vrata, a vow. Hindus keep vratas still, fasts and promises made with devotion. Before the first throw, a king's vow walks him to the board.
Your line: keeping a rule isn't the same as dharma. A vow can hold you up, or walk you to the board. Until tomorrow.

768.title: I have won
768.hook: stake after stake, Shakuni says I have won, and Vidura warns that the winner is in danger too
768.carry: where dharma is, there is victory
768.howItsDone: Vidura's warnings in the dice hall are a place where teachers and storytellers often pause, and his image of the honey-gatherer is retold as a picture of desire that can't see its own danger.

segments.voice: Yesterday, before the first throw: a warning, a dare, a vow, and a pearl set in gold, lost. Keeping a rule isn't the same as dharma.

There's a line in this part of the poem that keeps coming back, like a drumbeat. Yudhishthira names a stake. Shakuni throws. And then Shakuni says, in effect: I have won. Then again. And again. The poem repeats it until the words themselves begin to sound like a warning. And one man in the hall stands up and tries to stop it.
screen: `A LINE LIKE A DRUMBEAT.` → `I HAVE WON.` → `ONE MAN TRIES TO STOP IT.`

segments.voice: After the pearl, Yudhishthira reaches for the next stake. Treasure. Gold. A fine chariot. Servants. Elephants. Horses. Soldiers. Each time he describes the stake carefully, almost proudly. Each time the throw goes to Shakuni, and the same short line follows: I have won. The refrain takes the suspense away. We stop asking who wins the throw, and start asking: why doesn't he stop? Vidura asks it out loud. He turns to the blind king with a picture: a man climbs high after honey, so taken with it that he doesn't see the fall in front of him. That, he says, is your son. Stop the game while there's a family left to save. Duryodhana answers with scorn, and the king says nothing that stops it. Notice: the honey picture isn't about the loser. It's about the winner. Now the teaching. The Mahabharata has a line that comes back again and again, and India's Supreme Court took it as its motto: yato dharmas tato jayah, where dharma is, there is victory. It's the epic's answer to Shakuni's refrain. A throw can be won by trickery. A kingdom can be taken. But in the Hindu view, that isn't victory, because it's won against dharma, and the fruit of it is still coming. Duryodhana's hands are full of honey, and he's walking toward the edge. For today: a win that costs you dharma, a test passed by cheating, an argument won by cruelty, is the kind Vidura warned about. Ask not only did I win, but was dharma with me.

769.title: The last stakes
769.hook: the brothers are staked one by one, then Yudhishthira himself, then Draupadi, and the oldest Hindu scripture already warned against it
769.carry: the rig veda: play not with dice
769.howItsDone: The last stakes of the dice game are read aloud and staged as a turning point of the epic, and many Hindu teachers set them beside the Rig Veda's gambler's hymn as a warning about the dice.

segments.voice: Yesterday, stake after stake, the drumbeat of I have won, and Vidura's man reaching for honey. Where dharma is, there is victory.

Every treasure is gone. In the telling, Yudhishthira stakes his herds, his lands, his city, even the ornaments the princes wear. Lost, every one. And then the game changes from a matter of things to a matter of people. Shakuni asks: is there anything left? There is. Sitting near Yudhishthira, listening to all of it, are his four brothers.
screen: `EVERY TREASURE IS GONE.` → `IS THERE ANYTHING LEFT?` → `HIS FOUR BROTHERS.`

segments.voice: Yudhishthira stakes Nakula, one of the twins. Shakuni wins. He stakes Sahadeva. Lost. Then Shakuni tries something sly: the twins are Madri's sons; surely Kunti's sons, Bhima and Arjuna, are dearer to you. An attempt to split the brothers. Yudhishthira catches it: you're trying to divide us, and that's wrong. Then, as if to prove they can't be divided, he stakes Arjuna. Lost. Bhima. Lost. Himself. Lost. Shakuni says one stake is left: Draupadi. And Yudhishthira stakes her. The elders break into a sweat. Vidura holds his head in his hands. The blind king keeps asking whether the throw is won. Shakuni throws, and wins. Now the teaching. Hindu scripture saw this coming long before the epic. In the Rig Veda, the oldest Hindu scripture, there's a hymn in the voice of a gambler. He says the dice pull at him like a drink he cannot refuse; his wife, who never wronged him, pushes him away; his own family won't know him. And the hymn ends, in effect: play not with dice; till your field. That's why Hindu law books count dice among the vices, not the pastimes: not because a game is wicked, but because the dice ask for more and more, until the stakes are people. Yudhishthira's loyalty to his brothers was real, and the dice took that too. For today: anything that keeps asking you to stake a little more, an app, a bet, a habit, is the hymn's dice. Plough your field instead.

The game is over, and Duryodhana wants Draupadi brought into the hall. First he tells Vidura to fetch her. Vidura refuses flatly. In the telling, he says she can't have become anyone's slave, because Yudhishthira staked her after he'd already lost himself. Hold on to that; it's the thread of everything that follows. So Duryodhana turns to an usher, a servant whose job is carrying messages, and sends him to the women's rooms.
screen: `VIDURA REFUSES TO FETCH HER.` → `HE LOST HIMSELF FIRST.` → `A MESSENGER AT HER DOOR.`

segments.voice: The usher tells Draupadi that Yudhishthira, carried away by the game, has lost her, and she must come. Draupadi doesn't come. She sends him back with one thing to ask the gambler in the hall: whom did you lose first, yourself or me? If he lost himself first, he was no longer free when he staked her, and perhaps had nothing left to stake. She isn't pleading. She's asking for the facts the whole claim rests on. The usher asks it in the hall. Yudhishthira says nothing; the telling says he sits as if he's lost his senses. Duryodhana says: let her come and ask it herself. Draupadi sends the usher again, this time with a question for everyone: ask the assembly what is right for me to do. The usher hesitates to go a third time, so Duryodhana sends his brother Duhshasana. Now the teaching. In Hindu tradition, dharma isn't something you swallow in silence. It is asked about, argued, and answered. The Upanishads are full of students questioning teachers; the Gita itself is Arjuna's questions to Krishna. And Draupadi, staked and summoned, does the most dharmic thing in the hall: she asks what dharma is here, and makes the elders face it. Many Hindus still name her each morning in a short verse honoring five great women. For today: when something is done to you, or in your name, asking respectfully on what grounds is not disrespect. It's dharma too.
